# Solution

**Answer: No.** The condition does not imply the existence of such an injective function. We give a counterexample.

## Counterexample

Let $X = \mathbb{N} \cup \{p\}$, where $p$ is any set not belonging to $\mathbb{N}$ (for instance, $p = \{\mathbb{N}\}$). Define $F: X \to \mathcal{P}(X)$ by
$$F(p) = \mathbb{N}, \qquad F(n) = \{n\} \text{ for each } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

## Claim 1: Hall's condition holds

For every $A \subseteq X$, we have $|A| \le \left|\bigcup_{x \in A} F(x)\right|$.

*Proof.* Fix $A \subseteq X$ and set $N(A) = \bigcup_{x \in A} F(x)$.

**Case 1: $p \notin A$.** Then $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, and $N(A) = \bigcup_{n \in A}\{n\} = A$, so $|A| \le |A|$. ✓

**Case 2: $p \in A$.** Write $A = \{p\} \cup B$ with $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. Then
$$N(A) = F(p) \cup \bigcup_{n \in B} F(n) = \mathbb{N} \cup B = \mathbb{N},$$
so $|N(A)| = |\mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0$. Since $A \subseteq X = \mathbb{N} \cup \{p\}$, we have $|A| \le |X| = \aleph_0$. Hence $|A| \le \aleph_0 = |N(A)|$. ✓

In both cases the condition is satisfied. $\square$

## Claim 2: No injective choice function exists

There is no injective $f: X \to X$ with $f(x) \in F(x)$ for all $x \in X$.

*Proof.* Suppose for contradiction that such an $f$ exists. For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$f(n) \in F(n) = \{n\},$$
so $f(n) = n$. Since $f$ is injective, $f(p) \notin \{f(n) : n \in \mathbb{N}\} = \mathbb{N}$. But $f(p) \in F(p) = \mathbb{N}$, giving $f(p) \in \mathbb{N}$ and $f(p) \notin \mathbb{N}$ simultaneously — a contradiction. $\square$

## Conclusion

The set $X = \mathbb{N} \cup \{p\}$ with $F(p) = \mathbb{N}$ and $F(n) = \{n\}$ satisfies $|A| \le \left|\bigcup F(A)\right|$ for every $A \subseteq X$, yet admits no injective $f: X \to X$ with $f(x) \in F(x)$.

**Why the condition fails to suffice.** Cardinal arithmetic for infinite sets identifies $|X| = |\mathbb{N} \cup \{p\}| = |\mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0$, so the "one-element deficit" $\bigcup F(X) = \mathbb{N} \subsetneq X$ is invisible to the cardinality inequality $|X| \le |N(X)|$. Yet structurally, the element $p$ can only be sent into $\mathbb{N}$, which is already entirely consumed by the forced assignments $f(n)=n$. The finite Hall's marriage theorem detects such deficits (a finite set minus one element has strictly smaller cardinality), but for infinite sets the cardinality condition $|A| \le |N(A)|$ is too coarse — it cannot distinguish $N(A)$ from $N(A) \cup \{\text{one point}\}$ when $N(A)$ is infinite.

**Answer: No.** The condition does not imply the existence of such an injective function. We give a counterexample.

## Counterexample

Let $X = \mathbb{N} \cup \{p\}$, where $p$ is any set not belonging to $\mathbb{N}$ (for instance, $p = \{\mathbb{N}\}$). Define $F: X \to \mathcal{P}(X)$ by
$$F(p) = \mathbb{N}, \qquad F(n) = \{n\} \text{ for each } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

## Claim 1: Hall's condition holds

For every $A \subseteq X$, we have $|A| \le \left|\bigcup_{x \in A} F(x)\right|$.

*Proof.* Fix $A \subseteq X$ and set $N(A) = \bigcup_{x \in A} F(x)$.

**Case 1: $p \notin A$.** Then $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, and $N(A) = \bigcup_{n \in A}\{n\} = A$, so $|A| \le |A|$. ✓

**Case 2: $p \in A$.** Write $A = \{p\} \cup B$ with $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. Then
$$N(A) = F(p) \cup \bigcup_{n \in B} F(n) = \mathbb{N} \cup B = \mathbb{N},$$
so $|N(A)| = |\mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0$. Since $A \subseteq X = \mathbb{N} \cup \{p\}$, we have $|A| \le |X| = \aleph_0$. Hence $|A| \le \aleph_0 = |N(A)|$. ✓

In both cases the condition is satisfied. $\square$

## Claim 2: No injective choice function exists

There is no injective $f: X \to X$ with $f(x) \in F(x)$ for all $x \in X$.

*Proof.* Suppose for contradiction that such an $f$ exists. For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$f(n) \in F(n) = \{n\},$$
so $f(n) = n$. Since $f$ is injective, $f(p) \notin \{f(n) : n \in \mathbb{N}\} = \mathbb{N}$. But $f(p) \in F(p) = \mathbb{N}$, giving $f(p) \in \mathbb{N}$ and $f(p) \notin \mathbb{N}$ simultaneously — a contradiction. $\square$

## Conclusion

The set $X = \mathbb{N} \cup \{p\}$ with $F(p) = \mathbb{N}$ and $F(n) = \{n\}$ satisfies $|A| \le \left|\bigcup F(A)\right|$ for every $A \subseteq X$, yet admits no injective $f: X \to X$ with $f(x) \in F(x)$.

**Why the condition fails to suffice.** Cardinal arithmetic for infinite sets identifies $|X| = |\mathbb{N} \cup \{p\}| = |\mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0$, so the "one-element deficit" $\bigcup F(X) = \mathbb{N} \subsetneq X$ is invisible to the cardinality inequality $|X| \le |N(X)|$. Yet structurally, the element $p$ can only be sent into $\mathbb{N}$, which is already entirely consumed by the forced assignments $f(n)=n$. The finite Hall's marriage theorem detects such deficits (a finite set minus one element has strictly smaller cardinality), but for infinite sets the cardinality condition $|A| \le |N(A)|$ is too coarse — it cannot distinguish $N(A)$ from $N(A) \cup \{\text{one point}\}$ when $N(A)$ is infinite.
